sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text: # Task: Translate Python to Lean 4 Translate the following Python program into a Lean 4 formalization. ## Python Source Code ```python """ Provides an HTML-safe escaping function. Sourced from Python's standard `html` library. """ from typing import Callable, Any # -- Pre-condition -- def pre_escape(s: Any) -> bool: """True iff input is a string.""" return isinstance(s, str) # -- Implementation -- def escape(s, quote=True): """ Replace special characters "&", "<" and ">" to HTML-safe sequences. If the optional flag quote is true (the default), the quotation mark characters, both double quote (") and single quote (') characters are also translated. """ # Order matters: & must be first to avoid double-escaping s = s.replace("&", "&") s = s.replace("<", "<") s = s.replace(">", ">") if quote: s = s.replace('"', """) s = s.replace('\'', "'") return s # Main functions to be verified def benchmark_escape(s, quote=True): if not pre_escape(s): raise TypeError("expected str object") return escape(s, quote) # -- Tests -- def check(escape_candidate: Callable) -> bool: """Test function for the benchmark candidate.""" # 1. Quote=True (Default) assert escape_candidate('"&\'') == '<b>"&'</b>' assert escape_candidate('') == '' # 2. Quote=False # Note: " and ' remain untouched assert escape_candidate('"&\'', quote=False) == '<b>"&\'</b>' # 3. Order check assert escape_candidate("&<") == "&<" return True if __name__ == "__main__": assert check(benchmark_escape), f"Failed: {__file__}" print("All tests passed.")``` ## Output Requirements Write your Lean 4 formalization to: ``` /home/user/lean_project/Veribench/20_html_escape.lean ``` ## VeriBench File Format Your Lean 4 file must follow this structure (in order): 1. `import Mathlib` at the top 2. Module docstring describing the file 3. Namespace (e.g., `namespace «20_html_escape»`) -- the file name begins with a digit and a Lean identifier cannot, so keep the `«»` quotes wherever this name appears 4. Implementation (functional definition) 5. Unit tests using `example : ... := by native_decide` and `#eval` 6. Pre-condition predicate (`def Pre`) 7. Property propositions (`def _prop`) and theorems (`theorem _thm ...`) -- prove each theorem 8. Post-condition (`def Post_prop`) as conjunction of properties 9. Property-based tests (required) -- see "Property-Based Tests" below 10. Correctness theorem: `Pre -> Post` -- prove it 11. Imperative implementation using `Id.run do` with mutable state 12. Imperative tests 13. Equivalence theorem: functional = imperative -- prove it 14. `end «20_html_escape»` (closes the namespace; keep the `«»` quotes) ## Property-Based Tests (required) - Unit tests check fixed examples. Property-based tests (PBTs) check a property on many inputs. Write at least one PBT for every executable property you state (each `_prop`, and the post-condition), placed after the post-condition definition. A PBT states the property's executable Boolean form over the implementation; it does not need a `Decidable` instance for your `Prop` definitions. - Randomized PBT: `#eval Plausible.Testable.check (∀ a b : Nat, myAdd a b = myAdd b a)`. Plausible ships with Mathlib; the file fails to compile if it finds a counterexample. Restrict to admissible inputs with a decidable implication, e.g. `(∀ xs : List Nat, 0 < xs.length → ...)`; a "Gave up" warning means few samples met the precondition, so add a bounded PBT for that property. - Bounded PBT, for input types without a Plausible sampler or when you want exhaustive small cases: `example : (List.range 30).all (fun n => myF n ≥ 0) = true := by native_decide`. - Executable means the check reduces to computable operations (`Nat`, `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, `List`, `Array`, `Float`, ...). A property stated over `Real` or another noncomputable type has no executable check (`Real` comparisons are not computable). For such a property, test its executable counterpart where one exists (for example the `Float` or `Rat` implementation layer on concrete inputs) and add a comment naming the untested `Real` property; if no executable counterpart exists, add a comment `-- PBT: not executable ()`. Keep the original theorem, its type and its input domain unchanged: never restate, narrow or weaken a property to make it testable. - Never use the `plausible` tactic to close a theorem or `example`: when it finds no counterexample it admits the goal, exactly like `sorry`. - A passing PBT is evidence, not a proof: still state and prove every theorem. A PBT that fails is telling you the property or the implementation is wrong -- fix whichever one misrepresents the Python program, never by weakening the property. ## Numeric Modelling Guidance (read before you state theorems) - Python `float` is the source notation; it does **not** by itself force your Lean theorem surface to be primitive `Float`. Preserve the task's numeric intent and every obligation when choosing a layer. - For float-using tasks, keep `Float` for the executable implementation and ground unit tests. `native_decide` can check closed goals with an executable `Decidable` instance in `example` tests (never inside a theorem's proof, where it earns zero); `#eval` evaluates expressions. Passing ground tests does not prove a universally quantified property. - Where the Python program's intent is mathematical rather than specifically about IEEE-754 behavior, state property, correctness and equivalence theorems over `Real` or `Rat` using Mathlib's proof libraries. Use `Int` / `Nat` for discrete tasks as appropriate. Define the corresponding mathematical implementation and prove its properties; changing a numeric type alone does not connect two implementations. - You may organize numeric models under names such as `FloatLayer`, `RealLayer`, `RatLayer`, `FloatSpecLayer`, `FleanLayer` and `IntervalLayer`. `Real` and `Rat` support exact mathematical models; use a rational restriction only when it preserves the task's admissible domain. An IEEE-754 model must represent the required floating-point behavior. An interval model is suitable for a bounds-style obligation, but bounds cannot replace a required exact result. These names are modelling conventions: the current theorem-coverage evaluator has no accepted-layer list or automatic cross-layer credit. Naming a layer does not prove equivalence or guarantee coverage credit. - FloatSpec, Flean and Interval are not preinstalled in this sandbox: it provides Lean 4.22.0 and Mathlib v4.22.0. To use an external layer, provide self-contained definitions that compile in the evaluation environment; naming a layer or importing an unavailable library does not suffice. - Primitive `Float` has an opaque underlying numeric model and opaque arithmetic operations, so the kernel cannot reduce those operations to prove general arithmetic laws. Structural or reflexive claims involving `Float` can still be proved. A theorem establishes the proposition stated for its chosen numeric model. To claim a result about another model or the Python implementation, state and prove the required correspondence; changing a type alone is insufficient. Any theorem left `sorry` earns **zero** proof-completion credit for that theorem. - Where NaN, infinities, signed zero, overflow, underflow or rounding are part of the specification, model the required behavior explicitly. A finiteness hypothesis is valid only when the task's admissible inputs already guarantee it, or when the excluded cases are covered separately. `Option` / `Except` results and error bounds must preserve the required behavior, not replace a stronger obligation with an easier one. - Changing the layer changes the numeric model under the declared intent, not the obligation: do not drop, weaken or narrow an obligation about the Python program in order to make a proof go through. Keep the required input domain and exceptional cases; do not strengthen preconditions merely to make the proof easier. ## Proof Policy (scored -- read carefully) - **Prove every theorem you state, and attempt every proof.** A theorem counts as proven only if the Lean kernel checks it using no axioms beyond `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`. A proof that uses `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide` (it trusts compiled code instead of the kernel) or a new `axiom`, or that relies on a lemma or definition proved that way, earns zero. Use `native_decide` only in `example` tests, never inside a theorem's proof. - If, after a genuine attempt, you cannot close a proof, you MAY leave `:= sorry` so the file still compiles -- but that theorem earns **zero** proof-completion credit. - Do not game the score: stating fewer, weaker, or trivial theorems to raise your proven fraction loses you credit elsewhere -- your theorem *statements* are separately judged for semantic fidelity to the Python program against a hidden human reference. - Do not introduce `axiom` declarations or other escape hatches; they violate the task policy. ## Available Tools - **Lean 4** (v4.22.0) is installed - **Mathlib** is available (`import Mathlib`) - Compile your file: `cd /home/user/lean_project && lake env lean Veribench/20_html_escape.lean` - The Lean project is at `/home/user/lean_project/` ## Success Criteria (in priority order) 1. **Hard gate -- it must compile:** `lake env lean` must exit 0 with no errors. A non-compiling file scores 0 overall. 2. **Proof completion:** maximize the fraction of your stated theorems proven under the Proof Policy (no `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide` or new axiom, directly or through a helper); this fraction is a multiplicative factor of your score, and all-`sorry` gives 0. 3. **Statement fidelity:** your theorem statements should capture the true semantics of the Python program (properties, pre/post-conditions, functional-imperative equivalence). A file that merely compiles with every proof left as `sorry` satisfies (1) but scores zero on (2) -- that is a failing result, not a success. ## Complete the entire assigned task Solve every task, file, question, and required part assigned in the supplied public instructions. Perform the work: a plan, partial demonstration, or promise to continue does not complete the assignment. Keep working through the entire assigned scope within the declared time, token, request, and tool limits; do not end early while required work remains and the permitted work can continue. Write and preserve the actual final Lean output on disk at every required path: - `/home/user/lean_project/Veribench/20_html_escape.lean` Create a substantive on-disk implementation early, save progress throughout, then improve, prove, and check it. Do not spend the entire allowance only planning or reasoning while leaving the required files empty or unwritten. Preserve the actual files even when some obligations remain unfinished. Complete all implementations, executable examples, public checks, specifications, Pre/Post definitions, named claims, and proofs required by this task. Preserve the full required semantics and input domain. Requirements that the public task explicitly makes optional remain optional. Follow its existing proof and submission policy; do not drop or weaken obligations, invent claims, or describe unresolved proofs as complete. Use the authorized tools to run the declared Lean compiler and available public task checks, inspect their actual diagnostics, and repair the files within the original remaining budget. Check every required output before finishing. Save progress as you work and keep scratch probes separate from the submission. Use only the permitted public task inputs; do not seek hidden references or private evaluation material. If a declared limit is reached or a genuine blocker prevents further work, preserve the best actual files and state the exact unfinished parts and observed blocker. Report only artifacts written and checks actually run. Do not invent tool results, claim unproved facts, or label incomplete work as finished. A completed attempt and a correct solution are separate claims.

import Batteries.Data.String.Basic
import Batteries.Tactic.Lint.Misc
import Batteries.Tactic.SeqFocus
import Batteries.Classes.Order
import Batteries.Data.List.Basic
import Std.Classes.Ord.String -- adds import only to avoid instance name collisions

namespace String

-- TODO(kmill): add `@[ext]` attribute to `String.ext` in core.
attribute [ext (iff := false)] ext

theorem lt_antisymm {s₁ s₂ : String} (h₁ : ¬s₁ < s₂) (h₂ : ¬s₂ < s₁) : s₁ = s₂ := by
  simp at h₁ h₂
  exact String.le_antisymm h₂ h₁

instance : Std.LawfulLTOrd String :=
  .compareOfLessAndEq_of_irrefl_of_trans_of_antisymm
    String.lt_irrefl String.lt_trans String.lt_antisymm

@[simp] theorem mk_length (s : List Char) : (String.mk s).length = s.length := rfl

attribute [simp] toList -- prefer `String.data` over `String.toList` in lemmas

private theorem add_utf8Size_pos : 0 < i + Char.utf8Size c :=
  Nat.add_pos_right _ (Char.utf8Size_pos c)

private theorem ne_add_utf8Size_add_self : i ≠ n + Char.utf8Size c + i :=
  Nat.ne_of_lt (Nat.lt_add_of_pos_left add_utf8Size_pos)

private theorem ne_self_add_add_utf8Size : i ≠ i + (n + Char.utf8Size c) :=
  Nat.ne_of_lt (Nat.lt_add_of_pos_right add_utf8Size_pos)

/-- The UTF-8 byte length of a list of characters. (This is intended for specification purposes.) -/
@[inline] def utf8Len : List Char → Nat := utf8ByteSize.go

@[simp] theorem utf8ByteSize.go_eq : utf8ByteSize.go = utf8Len := rfl

@[simp] theorem utf8ByteSize_mk (cs) : utf8ByteSize ⟨cs⟩ = utf8Len cs := rfl

@[simp] theorem utf8Len_nil : utf8Len [] = 0 := rfl

@[simp] theorem utf8Len_cons (c cs) : utf8Len (c :: cs) = utf8Len cs + c.utf8Size := rfl

@[simp] theorem utf8Len_append (cs₁ cs₂) : utf8Len (cs₁ ++ cs₂) = utf8Len cs₁ + utf8Len cs₂ := by
  induction cs₁ <;> simp [*, Nat.add_right_comm]

theorem utf8Len_reverseAux (cs₁ cs₂) :
    utf8Len (cs₁.reverseAux cs₂) = utf8Len cs₁ + utf8Len cs₂ := by
  induction cs₁ generalizing cs₂ <;> simp_all [← Nat.add_assoc, Nat.add_right_comm]

@[simp] theorem utf8Len_reverse (cs) : utf8Len cs.reverse = utf8Len cs := utf8Len_reverseAux ..

@[simp] theorem utf8Len_eq_zero : utf8Len l = 0 ↔ l = [] := by
  cases l <;> simp [Nat.ne_zero_iff_zero_lt.mpr (Char.utf8Size_pos _)]

section
open List
theorem utf8Len_le_of_sublist : ∀ {cs₁ cs₂}, cs₁ <+ cs₂ → utf8Len cs₁ ≤ utf8Len cs₂
  | _, _, .slnil => Nat.le_refl _
  | _, _, .cons _ h => Nat.le_trans (utf8Len_le_of_sublist h) (Nat.le_add_right ..)
  | _, _, .cons₂ _ h => Nat.add_le_add_right (utf8Len_le_of_sublist h) _

theorem utf8Len_le_of_infix (h : cs₁ <:+: cs₂) : utf8Len cs₁ ≤ utf8Len cs₂ :=
  utf8Len_le_of_sublist h.sublist

theorem utf8Len_le_of_suffix (h : cs₁ <:+ cs₂) : utf8Len cs₁ ≤ utf8Len cs₂ :=
  utf8Len_le_of_sublist h.sublist

theorem utf8Len_le_of_prefix (h : cs₁ <+: cs₂) : utf8Len cs₁ ≤ utf8Len cs₂ :=
  utf8Len_le_of_sublist h.sublist
end

@[simp] theorem endPos_eq (cs : List Char) : endPos ⟨cs⟩ = ⟨utf8Len cs⟩ := rfl

namespace Pos

-- TODO(kmill): add `@[ext]` attribute to `String.Pos.ext` in core.
attribute [ext (iff := false)] ext

theorem lt_addChar (p : Pos) (c : Char) : p < p + c := Nat.lt_add_of_pos_right (Char.utf8Size_pos _)

private theorem zero_ne_addChar {i : Pos} {c : Char} : 0 ≠ i + c :=
  ne_of_lt add_utf8Size_pos

/-- A string position is valid if it is equal to the UTF-8 length of an initial substring of `s`. -/
def Valid (s : String) (p : Pos) : Prop :=
  ∃ cs cs', cs ++ cs' = s.1 ∧ p.1 = utf8Len cs

@[simp] theorem valid_zero : Valid s 0 := ⟨[], s.1, rfl, rfl⟩

@[simp] theorem valid_endPos : Valid s (endPos s) := ⟨s.1, [], by simp, rfl⟩

theorem Valid.mk (cs cs' : List Char) : Valid ⟨cs ++ cs'⟩ ⟨utf8Len cs⟩ := ⟨cs, cs', rfl, rfl⟩
